measurement.happened:
The single dominant story of the week in China was the Nvidia spy scandal. Jensen Huang was reported to have had a romantic affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman the US believes was a Chinese spy who spent years in Nvidia's orbit and pitched AI chip deals to investors. Nvidia launched an internal investigation, Huang admitted the affair, and the company's shares fell. China's Foreign Ministry called the whole episode baseless smears and slander, while Trump publicly backed Huang. Key Republican lawmakers demanded a briefing from Huang over the Chinese spy allegations, and the US Treasury and Commerce raised compliance concerns. Bloomberg ran a piece titled Everything Jensen Huang Said About China Is Out the Window, and multiple outlets noted that Nvidia ordered its data-center clients to reduce China exposure. Chinese media and the public were visibly angry at what they saw as a US smear campaign. This story touched every corner of the US-China tech relationship and will likely shape chip policy and trade talks for months. (Headlines: Reuters, AP, AFP, BBC, CNN, Deutsche Welle, TV5Monde, Bloomberg, WSJ, FT, CNBC, Al Jazeera.)

The second major theme was the extension of the US-China trade truce and related measures. China extended the suspension of new rare earth export controls until January, extended the pause on US tariffs and trade curbs by two months, extended the suspension of port fees on US-linked ships, and extended the sanctions suspension on South Korea's Hanwha Ocean by two months. The US, meanwhile, urged China to immediately meet its rare earths and agriculture commitments under the Busan deal, and Treasury Secretary Bessent and Trade Representative Greer raised compliance concerns. China said US farm purchases hinge on a tariff-cut deal, and it kept anti-dumping and anti-subsidy tariffs on US n-propanol imports for five more years. The US also targeted China-based suppliers in its escalation against Cuba. The overall tone was one of cautious continuation rather than a new breakthrough. (Headlines: Reuters, Bloomberg, FT, CNBC, Al Jazeera, Deutsche Welle.)

China's domestic economy and markets were a third major theme. Producer inflation (PPI) hit its highest level in over four years at 5.7 percent, while consumer inflation (CPI) moderated. The National Team, China's state-linked trading entities, ramped up ETF buying to a record high to stabilize the stock market. Beijing halted new IPO listings to protect the market from the AI-driven selloff, and the State Council called for stronger stock market stability. The central bank tweaked forex reserve rules and Chinese banks boosted dollar deposit rates to smooth the yuan's rally. The NDRC flagged weak domestic demand as a key challenge. China's quants swung to losses after the October tech selloff, a top-rated firm faced sudden distress testing the rating crackdown, and bad-debt collectors are chasing roughly 100 million defaulters. China's car exports are forecast to slow from a supercharged pace, and Siemens Healthineers and BMW both reported weaker results partly due to China weakness. On the positive side, China's Q3 emissions posted the biggest drop since the pandemic, China is set to lead the world in energy investment in 2026, and China started marketing green bonds for debut sales in Canada. (Headlines: Reuters, Bloomberg, WSJ, FT, CNBC, Deutsche Welle, TV5Monde.)

Diplomacy and the upcoming APEC summit formed a fourth theme. Trump said he expects to meet Xi and Putin at the China APEC summit, and China confirmed discussions are underway on a historic three-way meeting. The US, Russia, and China are all discussing logistics. Japan is working to shield its leader Takaichi from any snub by Xi at the summit. Senior Chinese and North Korean officials met in Beijing to urge closer ties. China and Gabon elevated their relationship with pledges on mining and security. China warned the Philippines to be cautious over the South China Sea. Taiwan detained a Communist Party leader over alleged Chinese sponsorship in its mayoral election, and also shut its Papua New Guinea office and ended LNG buying, citing Chinese pressure. China disputed reports of an artillery shell found in PNG. Italy's prosecutors targeted a China-linked network accused of tracking a dissident. (Headlines: Reuters, AP, Bloomberg, FT, CNBC, Al Jazeera, Deutsche Welle.)

Technology and AI were a fifth theme. Apple's Intelligence AI service registered with China's regulator for use on tablets and laptops, marking the arrival of Apple AI tools in China after a two-year delay. China blocked SoftBank's 5.4-billion-dollar acquisition of ABB's robotics division, flexing control over AI tech, and SoftBank and ABB are now exploring a China carve-out to salvage the deal. China's top flash memory chipmaker is targeting more homegrown tools for a new factory. China's Moonshot AI lab turned to Europe for Nvidia Blackwell chip access amid US-China curbs. Beijing sought to bolster AI shares, and the US-China AI arms race was described as escalating. China's critical minerals dominance left the UK dangerously exposed, MPs warned, and China expanded its overseas mining stakes. The EU validated JD.com's acquisition of the second-largest stake in Fnac Darty. (Headlines: Reuters, Bloomberg, WSJ, FT, CNBC, Deutsche Welle, TV5Monde, AFP.)

Political and institutional moves formed a sixth theme. China shifted several former provincial leaders to the legislature in what was described as soft retirement. Former Politburo member Ma Xingrui was charged with taking bribes. Xi tapped a military hatchet man to rebuild China's army command. China raised its delegate count to 2,360 for the 2027 Party Congress. China passed a cross-border corruption law expanding the anti-graft drive, and adopted a law on Antarctic activities and environmental protection. In Macau, an ex-lawmaker was sentenced to jail in the territory's first national security trial. A pastor at a Beijing underground church was arrested. The Financial Times ran a piece on the perils of Xi Jinping's purge. (Headlines: Reuters, AP, Bloomberg, FT, BBC.)

Space and science were a smaller but notable theme. A Pakistani astronaut will join China's Shenzhou-24 mission and become the first foreigner on China's space station. China's swarm strategy for the space race was profiled. (Headlines: Reuters, AP, Al Jazeera, FT.)

Culture, sports, and society rounded out the week. Kylian Mbappe's Mao comments led to China contacting Real Madrid and LaLiga, and Chinese state TV pulled La Liga matches. Mone Chiba won the Cup of China in figure skating. Chinese giant pandas made their public debut at an Atlanta zoo. Chinese motorcycles are conquering Europe. A former elementary school teacher became the newest paper billionaire in China. China's marriage rate in the third quarter tumbled to an 18-year low. Hyrox fitness events took off in China. Chinese e-bikes boomed as fuel prices rose. A building fire in Taiyuan killed 14. Tropical Storm Champi battered Taiwan and Japan before nearing China. Two Uyghur men in Thailand pleaded not to be sent back to China. An Astellas employee imprisoned in China is to be released in December. (Headlines: Reuters, AP, AFP, BBC, CNBC, Al Jazeera, Deutsche Welle, TV5Monde.)
measurement.expected:
The Nvidia spy scandal will continue to dominate the news cycle in China. Almost certainly, Beijing will keep firing off statements calling the affair a smear, Chinese state media will run editorials, and the story will be a talking point in any US-China trade or tech negotiations this week. The internal investigation at Nvidia will likely produce more leaks and speculation. Chinese tech firms, especially those in AI and semiconductors, may use the story to push for more self-sufficiency. (Confidence: almost certain.)

The two-month trade truce extensions will be implemented and both sides will begin the compliance-checking process. Probable, the US will press China on rare earths shipments and agricultural purchases, and China will respond by pointing to the tariff-cut precondition. There will likely be at least one more round of public posturing from both sides, with the US Treasury and Trade Representative issuing statements and the Chinese Foreign Ministry responding. (Confidence: probable.)

APEC summit preparations will accelerate. Probable, Chinese authorities will begin the logistical and security build-up in the host city, including the tech megacity cleanup already under way. Diplomatic shuttles between Washington, Beijing, and Moscow will intensify as the three-way Trump-Xi-Putin meeting is confirmed or rescheduled. Japan will continue trying to position Takaichi for the summit. (Confidence: probable.)

China's stock market stabilization efforts will continue. Probable, the National Team will keep buying ETFs, new IPO halts or delays will be announced, and the State Council or CSRC will issue further guidance on market stability. The PPI inflation spike to 5.7 percent will generate policy discussion, with the NDRC and PBoC likely commenting on whether it signals genuine reflation or is a supply-side artifact. (Confidence: probable.)

Yuan management will remain a focus. Probable, the PBoC will continue tweaking forex rules and banks will adjust dollar deposit rates to keep the yuan in a comfortable band. Global yuan flows heading for a record year will be a talking point. (Confidence: probable.)

The SoftBank-ABB robotics carve-out negotiations will progress. Possible, both parties will announce a revised structure or at least confirm they are still in talks. China's regulatory stance on foreign ownership of robotics and AI hardware will be a point of friction. (Confidence: possible.)

Shenzhou-24 preparations will be visible. Possible, there will be pre-launch media events, crew training footage, or technical briefings, especially with the historic inclusion of a Pakistani astronaut. A full launch is less likely this specific week but the buildup will be public. (Confidence: possible.)

The cross-border corruption law and the Ma Xingrui bribery case will generate more coverage. Possible, additional names from the former provincial leadership cohort will be mentioned in connection with the soft retirement reshuffling. (Confidence: possible.)

South China Sea and border tensions will simmer. Possible, another incident or verbal exchange with the Philippines or India could surface, especially if the US is distracted by the Nvidia story and midterms. (Confidence: possible.)

Less likely surprises: A major fiscal stimulus package announced to counter weak domestic demand (Societe General said the economy is not weak enough to trigger one, but a surprise package is not impossible). A new round of US tariffs or a China counter-move on rare earths beyond the extended suspension. A visible South China Sea naval standoff or a new India-China border incident. A surprise political purge announcement beyond Ma Xingrui. A major tech regulation move, such as new rules on AI model approvals or data localization.

Things I would not bet on: A full-blown trade war restart with new tariff schedules within this single week. A major military confrontation in the South China Sea or Indian Ocean. A yuan currency crisis or a sharp devaluation. The Shenzhou-24 rocket actually launching (historically late November to December). A major change in China's leadership structure or an emergency Politburo session. A full repeal of the rare earth export controls. A China-led global fiscal stimulus. A major epidemic or natural disaster hitting the news cycle.

delta.motion: Between the two photographs, the Nvidia spy scandal grew from a secondary story into the single dominant narrative of the week. In the first photograph it was a reported suspicion, a denial from Beijing, and Nvidia's claim that the matter was 'investigated and debunked.' Eight days later, Jensen Huang had admitted a romantic affair with a Chinese businesswoman the US believes was a spy, Nvidia had launched an internal investigation, its shares had fallen, US lawmakers were demanding briefings, and Treasury and Commerce had raised formal compliance concerns. The story accelerated from rumor to confirmed scandal at a very fast pace, touching chip policy, trade talks, and the broader US-China AI rivalry all at once. The Mbappé-Mao cultural storm shrank sharply. It was the loudest, most-covered item in the first photograph, spanning at least ten outlets and a dozen headlines. By the second photograph it was one entry in a culture-and-sports roundup alongside a figure-skating trophy, a panda debut in Atlanta, and a motorcycle trend. The Sanrio-Hello Kitty episode, which had drawn a second wave of commentary in the first week, vanished entirely. The US-China trade lane shifted in character: the first photograph showed a flurry of new restrictions (FCC lab ban, biotech limits, telecom phone-number ban, truck-trailer tariffs) punctuated by a small thaw in wheat. The second photograph shows the opposite motion, a broad extension of the existing truce, with rare-earth export controls paused until January, tariff suspensions extended by two months, port-fee suspensions continued, and Hanwha Ocean sanctions held. The tone moved from new friction to cautious continuation, with both sides pressing on compliance rather than adding new measures. The economic picture became more complex rather than simply worse. The first photograph showed a contracting PMI and a wall of weak earnings from European and Japanese automakers. The second photograph revealed producer inflation at 5.7 percent, the highest in over four years, even as consumer inflation moderated. The government's response shifted from passive observation to active intervention: the National Team ramped ETF buying to a record, Beijing halted new IPO listings, the State Council called for stronger market stability, and the central bank tweaked forex-reserve rules. The party-politics thread continued but changed shape. The first photograph featured the plenum, 33 expulsions, and the Zhang Shengmin elevation. The second photograph shows the aftermath playing out in specific institutional moves: Ma Xingrui charged with bribery, a military hatchet man tapped to rebuild army command, a cross-border corruption law passed, the 2027 Party Congress delegate count raised to 2,360, and several former provincial leaders shifted to the legislature in soft retirement. The APEC summit, barely a footnote in the first photograph (an Australian PM visit was mentioned), grew into a major diplomatic event, with Trump saying he expects to meet Xi and Putin and all three sides discussing logistics for what could be a historic three-way meeting. New themes appeared that were absent or minor in the first photograph: Apple's Intelligence AI service registering with China's regulator after a two-year delay, China blocking SoftBank's 5.4-billion-dollar acquisition of ABB's robotics division, a Pakistani astronaut set to become the first foreigner on China's space station, a cross-border corruption law, an Antarctic activities law, a Macau national-security trial, China's green-bond debut in Canada, and the marriage rate falling to an 18-year low. Themes that were prominent in the first photograph and faded or vanished by the second include the formal German and Swiss diplomatic visits, the specific FCC and biotech ban headlines (absorbed into the broader truce extension), the Evergrande property-management sale, and the detailed list of US restrictions that had dominated the trade section.
delta.wind: On the Mbappé and cultural fallout, the expectation was that the saga would 'almost certainly' keep generating headlines and that more brand stumbles would appear. In reality the story did continue, with China contacting Real Madrid and La Liga and state TV pulling matches, but it shrank to a minor item in a broader culture section. The Sanrio second wave did not materialize, and no formal 'mutual respect' statement from a Chinese trade or cultural body appeared. The expectation was partially right in direction but overestimated the magnitude and duration. On party politics and purges, the forecast was largely correct. Additional names did appear (Ma Xingrui's bribery charge), further personnel moves materialized (the military command rebuild), and no major Politburo-level shakeup occurred, matching the 'unlikely' tag. The cross-border corruption law and the delegate-count increase were not explicitly predicted but fit the pattern of institutional consolidation the expectation described. On economic data and stimulus, the expectation of more weak data and possible modest stimulus was partially met but in a different form. The data was not uniformly weak; producer inflation actually hit a four-year high, complicating the simple deflation narrative. The government response was active stabilization (record ETF buying, IPO halt, forex tweaks) rather than the 'Japan-style stimulus' or PBOC rate cut that was floated. The 'almost certain' auto weakness continued, confirmed by BMW and Siemens Healthineers reporting China-driven softness. The expectation was directionally correct on the auto drag but missed the producer-inflation surprise and the active-market-management response. On US-China tech and trade, the expectation of a 'probable' formal retaliation over the FCC ban was not the headline; instead the truce was broadly extended and both sides pressed on compliance. The 'possible' additional Chinese export controls did not appear as new measures but were folded into the existing rare-earth pause. The 'unlikely' full trade-war escalation did not happen. The expectation got the tone right (cautious, simmering) but missed that the week's trade story would be about sustaining the truce rather than testing it. On the Nvidia spy plot, the expectation was that the story would 'probably' keep generating headlines and that China would point to the 'debunked' language. Both happened, but the story grew far beyond what was forecast. The affair revelation, the internal investigation, the lawmaker briefings, and the Treasury and Commerce compliance concerns represent a step toward the 'unlikely' formal US investigation. The expectation underestimated the speed at which a rumor could become a confirmed scandal with institutional consequences. On Taiwan and the South China Sea, the 'almost certain' continued patrols and the 'probable' Philippine statement both appeared, with China warning the Philippines to be cautious. The 'possible' new incident or warship transit did not dominate. The theme shrank relative to the first photograph, and the expectation was broadly correct but the maritime story was less prominent than forecast. On North Korea, the 'possible' missile test did not appear, and the 'unlikely' new high-level meeting was slightly exceeded, with senior officials meeting in Beijing to urge closer ties. The expectation was roughly right. On markets, the 'probable' volatility and the 'almost certain' European auto weakness both materialized. The 'possible' short-term rally on a stimulus hint did not quite happen; instead the government intervened directly with record ETF buying and an IPO halt. The expectation was close but the mechanism of support was more active than a simple rally. Among the 'less likely surprises,' the APEC three-way summit (Trump, Xi, Putin) was a bigger deal than the 'diplomatic meeting with a Western leader' that was listed. The Apple AI registration in China and the SoftBank-ABB robotics block were not in the expectations at all and were notable omissions. The large 2-trillion-yuan stimulus package did not appear as a single announcement, though the combination of IPO halt, record ETF buying, and forex tweaks served a similar stabilizing function. The WTO complaint and the new AI chip breakthrough did not materialize. Among the 'things I would not bet on,' the major military exercise, the full trade negotiation, the demographic policy change, the South China Sea arbitration shift, and the emergency rate cut all stayed absent, confirming those calls. The Tropical Storm Champi, which was noted as just having passed, did batter Taiwan and Japan before nearing China, a mild version of the 'major natural disaster' that was not bet on. Overall, the expectations framework was structurally sound for party politics, the trade tone, and the market direction, but it underweighted the speed of the Nvidia escalation, overweighted the Mbappé story's persistence, and missed the producer-inflation surprise and the active market-management response. The biggest systematic error was treating the US-China tech relationship as a series of discrete policy moves (FCC ban, biotech limits) when in reality the week's story was a single escalating human drama (the Nvidia affair) that subsumed the policy items.
delta.driver: The force pushing China from the first photograph to the second is the collision between an accelerating US-China AI-and-chip rivalry and a domestic economy that is simultaneously overheating in producer prices and cooling in consumer demand. The Nvidia affair crystallized what had been a grinding policy contest into a personal, emotional, and institutional crisis, forcing both governments to react in real time rather than in measured statements. At the same time, the fragile trade truce, extended but not deepened, created a narrow corridor in which both sides could manage the Nvidia fallout without triggering a full escalation. Domestically, the mixed inflation picture and the tech-stock selloff compelled the government to shift from watching the data to actively managing the market, halting IPOs, deploying record ETF buying, and tweaking forex rules. The party's institutional consolidation, the cross-border corruption law, the military command rebuild, and the 2027 Congress delegate count, all point to a leadership preparing its internal architecture for a longer power transition while projecting stability outward. The APEC summit and the prospect of a three-way Trump-Xi-Putin meeting add a diplomatic window that both sides want to exploit, giving the Nvidia storm a deadline and the trade truce a reason to hold. In short, the motion from one photograph to the next is driven by a single underlying tension: China trying to hold together a stable, confident, and institutionally consolidated front while the US presses on the exact technology (AI chips) that is central to its growth strategy, and the domestic economy sends mixed signals that demand active management rather than passive stimulus.

crystal.headline: APEC Three-Way Summit Looms as Nvidia Scandal Enters Investigation Phase
emoji_reasons: The China-hosted APEC summit with a possible Trump-Xi-Putin three-way meeting is the week's dominant diplomatic event and will set the tone for US-China relations for months.
The Nvidia spy scandal, now in its second week with a lawmaker briefing and internal investigation, remains the single most-covered story touching chip policy, trade, and the broader AI rivalry.

China's active market management, including record ETF buying, an IPO halt, and forex tweaks in response to the PPI surprise and tech-stock selloff, will continue to shape the domestic economic narrative.
crystal.tldr: Next week in China will be dominated by the APEC summit and the prospect of a historic Trump-Xi-Putin three-way meeting, which both sides will use to project stability and managed cooperation. The Nvidia spy scandal will enter its investigation phase, with Jensen Huang's lawmaker briefing and the 'reduce China exposure' order driving the US-China tech narrative. Domestically, the government will continue active market management rather than announce a large stimulus, as the PPI surprise at 5.7 percent complicates the policy picture.
crystal.eli5:
Next week, China is hosting a big international meeting called APEC, where the leaders of the US, China, and Russia might all sit at the same table for the first time in a while. Think of it like a school assembly where three loud kids who keep arguing in the hallway are finally put in the same room. Everyone will take photos, say nice things, and probably agree to keep talking. Nobody expects a perfect solution, but everyone wants to look like they're getting along.

At the same time, the big drama about the boss of Nvidia (the company that makes the computer chips for AI) and a Chinese woman who might have been a spy is still going. Next week, the boss has to go in front of lawmakers and explain what happened. It's like a student who was caught talking to a new kid in class, and now the principal wants to know if the new kid was actually a spy from the rival school. The whole thing is making both the US and China a little angry and a little nervous about who gets to build the smartest computers.

Back home in China, the economy is sending mixed signals. Factory prices went up a lot (which is usually a good thing, but it also means things are getting more expensive), while regular people are still not spending as much as they used to. The government is trying to keep the stock market from dropping by buying shares themselves, kind of like a parent quietly putting money in their kid's piggy bank so it doesn't look empty. They're not giving everyone a big bonus, but they're trying to make sure the piggy bank doesn't run out. There's also a lot of behind-the-scenes shuffling in the government, with some officials getting promoted, some getting retired, and a few getting in trouble for taking bribes. It's a lot like the student council at the end of the year, where some kids stay on and some get new jobs.

judgment.reading_a: Forecast A identified six themes and was broadly correct that US-China relations would dominate the news cycle, that the Nvidia spy story would generate a formal investigation and a Chinese counter-accusation, that the Mbappé saga would produce concrete follow-ups (Real Madrid/La Liga contact, state TV pulling matches), that economic and auto-industry pain would continue (BMW, Siemens Healthineers, Volvo all reported China weakness), that party-politics headlines would persist (Ma Xingrui charged, provincial leaders shifted to legislature, military hatchet man appointed), and that maritime/border tensions would continue (China warned Philippines, India-China border friction in Arunachal Pradesh). A's 'less likely surprises' list was notably accurate: a Western auto brand reporting China restructuring (BMW, Siemens), a second Nvidia development (multiple), a small Chinese market-stabilization measure (ETF buying, IPO halt), and a Chinese counter-accusation of espionage ('smears and slander'). A also correctly foresaw the 'AI bubble has popped in China' narrative and the tech-stock pressure. Where A was most wrong: it expected a 'formal, multi-item retaliation package' with tariffs on US agricultural goods and expanded export curbs, while the actual week was about extending the existing truce (rare earths suspension, tariff pause, port fees, Hanwha Ocean sanctions). The tone was cautious continuation, not escalation. A also expected the Australian PM visit to be a headline, but the diplomatic star was the Trump-Xi-Putin APEC discussions, which A did not mention. A's expectation of 'expanded export curbs on AI or semiconductor components' was partially right (SoftBank/ABB block, Moonshot seeking Blackwell via Europe) but not in the form described. A's 'what I would not bet on' list was mostly correct: no full trade truce (the truce was extended, not newly signed), no dramatic stimulus, no live-fire exercise, no Evergrande-scale default. The one partial miss was a 'major natural disaster' — Tropical Storm Champi did batter Taiwan and Japan before nearing China, though it was not a major disaster for China itself. Overall, A's picture was vivid and its specific predictions within each theme were largely accurate, with the main directional error being the trade-escalation framing.
judgment.reading_b: Forecast B used a probability framework (almost certain, probable, possible, unlikely) and covered Mbappé/cultural fallout, party politics, economic data, US-China tech and trade, the Nvidia spy plot, Taiwan/South China Sea, North Korea, and markets. B correctly identified that the Mbappé saga would continue to generate headlines and that Chinese social media would still be processing it, and that party-politics dissection would continue with additional names (Ma Xingrui) and personnel moves (military hatchet man, provincial leaders to legislature). B was right that European and Japanese automakers would report China weakness (BMW, Siemens, Volvo) and that markets would remain volatile with tech under pressure. B correctly said a full trade-war escalation was unlikely and that the tension would 'keep simmering.' B's Nvidia prediction was directionally correct (story continues, Chinese pointed statement) but it called a 'formal US investigation or indictment' unlikely, when in fact Nvidia launched an internal investigation and US lawmakers demanded a congressional briefing. B's biggest miss was on rare earths: it expected 'additional Chinese export controls on rare earths, gallium, or specific AI components as a counter-punch,' but China actually extended the suspension of new rare earth controls until January, which is the opposite — a relaxation, not a tightening. B also said a 'new high-level meeting' between China and North Korea was unlikely, yet senior officials from both sides met in Beijing to urge closer ties. B's North Korea missile-test prediction did not materialize. B's 'less likely surprises' list was reasonable: no large stimulus, no WTO complaint, no major new AI model release (though Apple Intelligence registration and the SoftBank block were AI-related headlines), and the Xi-Western-leader meeting was partially captured by the Trump-Xi-Putin discussions. B's 'things I would not bet on' were mostly correct: no major military exercise, no full trade summit, no demographic policy change, no SCS arbitration shift, no emergency rate cut. The Tropical Storm Champi miss was minor. Overall, B's picture was accurate in tone and broad strokes, but its probability labels occasionally misfired (rare earths, North Korea meeting, formal US investigation), and its predictions were less specific than A's, making it harder to see exactly what B thought would happen in concrete terms.
judgment.comparison: Both forecasts captured the dominant themes of the week: the Nvidia spy scandal as the single biggest story, the continuation of US-China trade tensions (albeit in a 'cautious continuation' mode rather than full escalation), economic weakness and market stabilization, party-politics follow-through, the Mbappé cultural-diplomatic saga, and ongoing maritime/border friction. Neither forecast predicted the Trump-Xi-Putin APEC three-way meeting discussions, which became a notable diplomatic headline. Neither predicted the Pakistani astronaut joining Shenzhou-24 as the first foreigner on China's space station, a small but distinctive headline. On the Nvidia story specifically, A's prediction was sharper and more accurate: A expected 'a formal US investigation announcement, a second name surfacing, or a Chinese counter-accusation,' and all three materialized (Nvidia internal investigation, Alice Huang as the named individual, China's 'baseless smears and slander' response). B said the story would 'continue to generate headlines' and that China might issue a pointed statement, which is correct but vaguer, and B called a formal US investigation 'unlikely,' which was a slight miss. On trade, A expected a 'formal multi-item retaliation package' with tariffs and export curbs, while the actual week was about extending the existing truce. B expected 'formal retaliation or at least a pointed statement' and 'additional export controls on rare earths,' but China extended the suspension of rare earth controls (the opposite of adding new ones). B's rare-earth error is a notable directional miss. On the cultural-diplomatic theme, both were correct that Mbappé would generate follow-ups, but A was more specific (Real Madrid/La Liga contact, state-media editorial, possible second cultural irritant), and the Real Madrid/La Liga contact and state TV match-pulling confirmed A's specifics. On economics, both were broadly right, but A's mention of the 'AI bubble has popped' narrative, the quants' losses, and the specific auto-brand pain (Volkswagen, Audi, Mercedes, Toyota) mapped more closely to the actual headlines (BMW, Siemens, Volvo, quants in losses, AI selloff). B's economic section was correct but less granular. On party politics, both were accurate; A's expectation of 'one or two additional personnel moves' was confirmed by Ma Xingrui's bribery charge, the provincial leaders' soft retirement, and the military hatchet man appointment. B's probability labels were clean but occasionally wrong (North Korea meeting 'unlikely' but it happened; formal US investigation 'unlikely' but it happened). A's 'less likely surprises' list was more on-target: Western auto brand restructuring (BMW, Siemens), second Nvidia development (multiple), small Chinese stimulus (market stabilization), Chinese counter-accusation (smears/slander). B's equivalent list was reasonable but less specific. In terms of serving a reader as a picture of the coming week, A's forecast was more vivid and its specific predictions hit more often, despite the trade-escalation framing being slightly off. B's forecast was more measured and its probability framework was cleaner, but its less-specific predictions and the rare-earth directional error made it a slightly less useful guide. The gap is narrow, but A's greater specificity and higher hit-rate on concrete predictions give it the edge.
